anchors.fact: At an upscale Mexican restaurant (p. 72 gives no city; the chain had Seattle and Portland branches, so guest text says "the Pacific Northwest", audit v1 H10), he worked his way up from busboy to bartender, mostly making frozen drinks, "and liked it" (*Proper* p. 72; P1).
anchors.meaning: An ordinary job, done gladly. Never "frozen Margaritas" (*For Good*'s).
anchors.speaksTo: the everyday side; no solo genius

anchors.fact: A customer ordered a Singapore Sling. He asked two senior bartenders, and nobody knew how to make it. The book says that "didn't sit right": he bought his first cocktail book at Powell's in Portland and "kept going back" (p. 72; P2). The night itself isn't placed (H10).
anchors.meaning: Someone asked, and nobody behind the bar could answer: that's the guest's mirror. Not his failure, and never the seniors' fault. The page doesn't say he later made that Sling, or found it in the book: "I like to think" at most. No year, no outcome for that guest.
anchors.speaksTo: fear: being the one who isn't enough when someone's counting on them; hides the hours nobody saw

anchors.fact: His collection grew to hundreds of volumes (three hundred on p. 60; he said 350 in 2010). In 2010 he said he'd learned more from watching other people work than from his books; asked about mentors: "Probably dozens… I take something from each person." (FoodGPS 2010; P3, P4).
anchors.meaning: The hours were real, and he hands the credit to the people around him, in his own words. Say "hundreds", never either number.
anchors.speaksTo: shares all the credit, keeps all the fear

anchors.fact: His own words, of a Friday night in the rush: sixteen drinks going, "a lot of it is still muscle memory", keeping track of who's next; "That moment where: I got this." (p. 75; P6).
anchors.meaning: The rush is the day that counts, and it comes every week. The drill is why it feels ordinary. It happens every week: never "the one night".
anchors.speaksTo: one true thing: what looks like calm is rehearsal; the practice holds

anchors.fact: Asked what he'd like to be known for: "making consistently excellent cocktails" (FoodGPS 2010; P5).
anchors.meaning: The same good drink every time, not the best one once.
anchors.speaksTo: anyone would have done the same; gives: the people near them are all right on the bad day

anchors.fact: Simonson says he could have become his city's star bartender but "didn't seize the mantle or seem to want it"; by the 2010s he stayed for years at one bar, long after its original staff had moved on, and "seemed most contented simply being a bartender" (p. 75; G1, G3).
anchors.meaning: Attributed, hedges kept. He stayed in the place; the crew left: never "stayed with his crew". His early cocky years get one clause at most (X1) and are never read onto the guest. No line says he never wanted attention.
anchors.speaksTo: being singled out feels like being left out; belonging

anchors.fact: Born Mark Johnson, he moved to Seattle at twenty-one and changed his name (the page dates the move, not the change); the surname came "from Greek mythology" (p. 71; N1). Dionysos is the ancient Greek god of wine (Mark Cartwright, *World History Encyclopedia*, 2012; secondary). He spells it Dionysos (N2).
anchors.meaning: Wren's ruling: one plain clause. He chose it, from the god of wine this place is named after. Never luck, never a joke, and nothing of his character read into it (the page's "more extroverted" reading stays in the dossier). **"God of wine" isn't on p. 71**: the page says only "Greek mythology", so the gloss rests on the encyclopedia, and the page gives no reason for the choice.
anchors.speaksTo: — (flag for Robin: second name coincidence in the family)

anchors.fact: The Sling is gin, liqueurs, citrus and soda, made across British Asia with plenty of latitude in the recipe. Its earliest recipe we have is a bar order printed in 1913, from the Singapore Cricket Club: "one Cherry Brandy, one Domb [i.e., Bénédictine], one Gin, one Lime Juice", ice, soda water, a few dashes of bitters (Oxford pdf 1803; *Imbibe!* pdf 122; S3, S11). From 1974 a Singapore hotel remade it with less Bénédictine and cherry, and added pineapple, orange and Cointreau; Oxford calls the result "sweet, rather sticky" (pdf 1804; S6–S7).
anchors.meaning: "The older way, before a hotel sweetened it in the 1970s." Never "the original", Raffles or Ngiam Tong Boon. Who ordered it: Oxford says "a member", *Imbibe!* says the younger members, so no number. One order that names the parts, never "one at a time" (my shorthand, struck, audit v1 H7). The club's refusal stays out.

anchors.fact: Spec v1: 30 ml each of London dry gin, Cherry Heering, Bénédictine and lime, built over one large cube in a large rocks glass, stirred, 90 ml soda, 3 dashes Angostura on top, no garnish. **The order's:** the four "one"s, ice, water, bitters (pdf 1803 / 122). **Wondrich's:** reading each "one" as 1 oz, the Singapore measure (*Imbibe!* pdf 122). **Ours:** the rocks glass and single cube (he says a Collins glass over ice), 90 ml soda (his 1–2 oz), three dashes, no garnish.
anchors.meaning: "I kept it at one measure of each": the equal measures are ours by Wondrich's reading, and the order itself says "one" of each. Never "his" Sling: p. 72 never says Dionysos made one.
anchors.speaksTo: practice so ordinary it needs no book; one of the crew

anchors.fact: Bénédictine is "essential" to the Singapore Sling among other classics (Oxford pdf 256); in the period it was "often replaced or supplemented by curaçao" (pdf 1803–1804). It's made from 27 plants and spices, nutmeg among them (pdf 256), so it counts as `nuts` on the safe side (S10).
anchors.meaning: "Goes into the Singapore Sling", never "always". The 1510 monk is company legend: out.

cocktail.closingLine: One of each, so anyone can learn it. Someone beside you already has.
cocktail.glassware: large rocks glass (about 400 ml), one large ice cube
method: Pour the gin, Cherry Heering, Bénédictine and lime juice straight into a large rocks glass: 30 ml of each.
Add one large ice cube and stir for about 20 seconds, until the outside of the glass feels cold.
Top up with the cold soda water and give it one gentle stir.
Shake three dashes of Angostura bitters onto the top. No garnish.
cocktail.name: Anyone Would Have

recipe.note: one of each: that's the whole recipe

recipe.item: Cherry Heering (recommended), or another red cherry liqueur
recipe.note: the red cherry brandy Singapore drank then; it's what turns the drink pink

recipe.item: Bénédictine (recommended), or another sweet herbal liqueur
recipe.note: a French liqueur of herbs and spices, finished with honey

cocktail.tagline: When it counts, you've already done it a hundred times.

reading.epigraph: Gin, cherry, herbs and lime. One day, nobody behind the bar could make it.
whoYouAre: The lights go out in the middle of a party, and you already know where the fuse box is. The car won't start on the way to the airport, and you've got the number saved. Afterwards, you shrug: anyone would have done the same. But you know that isn't quite true. You found the fuse box the week you moved in. You drove the route the day before. You don't trust yourself to be at your best on the day, so you don't leave anything to the day.

What you'd never say is why. It isn't pride. You're afraid of being the one who wasn't enough when someone was counting on you. So you practise, quietly, for things that may never happen, and when it goes well you hand the credit to everyone else. Being singled out has always felt a bit like being left out. But everyone near you gets through a bad day more easily because of a hundred ordinary ones you never mention. That's how you care for people, and it deserves more than a shrug.
yours: At a Mexican restaurant in the Pacific Northwest, Marco Dionysos worked his way up from clearing tables to the bar. (He chose that surname himself, after the Greek god of wine: the same god this place is named after.) There he mostly made frozen drinks, and liked it. Then one day a guest ordered a Singapore Sling. Marco asked two senior bartenders, and neither of them knew the recipe. As his story is told, that didn't sit right with him. He went to a bookshop in Portland, bought his first cocktail book, and kept going back.

His books ran into the hundreds, though he said he learned more from watching other people work. He moved to San Francisco and tended bar there for years. He once described a moment on a busy Friday night, with sixteen drinks going at once, a lot of it muscle memory, and the part he loved: "I got this." One writer says he could have become the city's star bartender, but "didn't seize the mantle or seem to want it". Asked what he'd like to be known for, Marco said "making consistently excellent cocktails". Asked about his mentors, he said: "Probably dozens."

That guest at the bar, waiting for a drink nobody there could make: I like to think he never quite forgot them. Nobody had done anything wrong. Someone had simply asked, and nobody was ready. I think that's the moment you practise against: not failing, but being the one who wasn't enough when it mattered. So you put in the hours nobody sees, and when the day comes and goes fine, you shrug. Like Marco, you'd rather be known for getting it right every time.

The cocktail I've made for you is that Singapore Sling, the older way, before a hotel sweetened it in the 1970s. The earliest recipe on record is a bar order from 1913, at a club in Singapore: one cherry brandy, one Bénédictine (a sweet herbal liqueur), one gin, one lime juice, then ice, soda water and some bitters. I kept it at one measure of each, so it's the kind of recipe you'll never need a book for. It's built straight in the glass over one big ice cube and stirred, with no shaker and nothing to show: a deep, rosy pink-red, a little cloudy with lime, the bitters just starting to bleed in from the top. I made it properly, for the guest who asked for it that day, and for every day you've got ready so nobody's left waiting.

You've spent years getting ready for other people's hard days. What you forget is that the others have been getting ready too, and some of it was for yours. Being enough was never meant to be your job alone. So before the next day like that, practise as much as you like. Then look at who's around you, and trust their hours the way they've always trusted yours. You were never the only one who was ready.
